definitions.definition: Dharma is the beneficial object (artha) marked by injunction: the enjoined act that joins a person with the highest good; perception cannot know it, and what the Veda states only as a means for harm (the Śyena) is not dharma.
An object with a purpose made known by the Veda — the sacrifice and the like (Arthasaṅgraha).

relations.note: dharma lies outside the reach of perception and the means based on it
the declared fruit of the paradigm rites

definitions.definition: The Vedic statement that impels to action; the sole means of knowing dharma, able to make known the future, subtle and remote.
What it conveys is bhāvanā, the prompting force (Kumārila); for Maṇḍana, that the act is a means to the desired (iṣṭasādhanatā).
What it conveys is the command / what is to be done (niyoga, kārya).
Originative (utpatti), applicatory (viniyoga), performative (prayoga) and eligibility (adhikāra) injunctions.

name: Injunction proper, restriction and exclusive specification

definitions.definition: An injunction enjoins what is otherwise not obtained at all (apūrva-vidhi), restricts to one of optional means (niyama) or, where something is obtained in several ways, excludes the others (parisaṅkhyā).

name: The fivefold division of the Veda

definitions.definition: The Veda consists of injunction (vidhi), mantra, name (nāmadheya), prohibition (niṣedha) and explanatory praise (arthavāda); all are meaningful through injunctions directly or indirectly.
The sūtra divides the Veda into mantra and brāhmaṇa (MS 2.1.32–33) and treats injunction, arthavāda, mantra, smṛti and name in adhyāya 1.

name: Arthavāda (explanatory praise and blame)

definitions.definition: Non-injunctive Vedic passages; without independent purpose, they serve injunctions by praise, forming one sentence with them (MS 1.2.1, 1.2.7); fruits stated for subsidiaries are arthavāda (MS 4.3.1).
Praise or blame; supplementing injunction or prohibition; figurative, restating, or fact-stating; praise, blame, another's deed, ancient narrative.

relations.note: arthavāda is one of the six marks of purport in Vedānta manuals, where it signals the passage's purport

notes: The reconciliation principle P7-arthavada in config/principles.md derives from this concept.

definitions.definition: The part of the Veda recited as prompting the performance; meaningful like any sentence against the objection that mantras are meaningless (MS 1.2.31–40, 2.1.32).
Mantras serve by recalling items connected with the performance.
Words in injunctions that name rites rather than enjoin qualities, recognized on four grounds.
A prohibition turns one away from harmful acts; where the negation cannot attach to the injunctive, it is an exclusion forming a positive vow of not-doing.

name: Apūrva (the unseen potency of ritual action)

definitions.definition: The perishable act produces an unseen potency that yields the enjoined fruit at a later time; its existence is known from the injunction itself (MS 2.1.5, Śabara).
Identified with the injunction's 'what is to be done' (kārya), known only from the Veda.

relations.note: the apūrva brings about heaven for one who desires it
Jaimini: dharma itself gives the fruit, not a lord (as reported in BS 3.2.40)

definitions.definition: The verbal suffix conveys bhāvanā: the injunction's prompting force (śābdī) and the agent's activity (ārthī), each with three expectancies — what, by what, how.

name: Niyoga / kārya (the command, what is to be done)

definitions.definition: The content of injunctions and the primary meaning of Vedic sentences: the act as to be done, identical with the apūrva, prompting the eligible person by itself.

relations.note: the rival Bhāṭṭa account of what the injunction conveys

name: Obligatory, occasional, desire-prompted and prohibited acts

definitions.definition: Nitya acts (lifelong) and naimittika acts (on occasions) are to be performed — they destroy past sin and avert the demerit of omission; kāmya acts bring their fruits and more births; niṣiddha acts bring demerit. The seeker of release does the first two and avoids the last two.
The seeker of release abstains from prohibited and desire-prompted acts, exhausts past karma by experience, and destroys it by self-knowledge with calm, restraint and celibacy.

Who may perform a rite and receive its fruit: humans, not animals or gods (MS 6.1.4–5); women as well as men, husband and wife jointly (MS 6.1.8, 6.1.17); for Vedic rites, those with Vedic learning, excluding śūdras (MS 6.1.25–38); the eligibility injunction states ownership of the fruit.

relations.note: Vedānta distinguishes the eligible for ritual from the eligible for Brahman-inquiry (P4-stage)

name: The adhikaraṇa method of interpretation

definitions.definition: Each topic is set out in five members — subject, doubt, connection, prima facie view, conclusion — and the conclusion becomes a maxim (nyāya) applied elsewhere.

notes: Some later manuals give 'nirṇaya' or 'prayojana' in place of saṅgati; the Nyāyamālā's own list is followed.

name: The six marks of purport (ṣaḍ-liṅga), as grounded in Mīmāṃsā

definitions.definition: Mīmāṃsā supplies the criteria that Vedānta manuals list as six marks: the opening and close of a passage (upakrama–upasaṃhāra; their relative strength argued in the Upakramaparākrama), repetition (abhyāsa, which marks a distinct rite, MS 2.2.2), novelty (apūrvatā: an injunction is for what is otherwise unobtained), the stated result (phala, MS 4.3), praise (arthavāda, MS 1.2.7) and reasoned demonstration (upapatti); doubtful sense is settled by the complementary passage (MS 1.4.29).

notes: The versified list 'upakramopasaṃhārāv abhyāso 'pūrvatā phalam / arthavādopapattī ca liṅgaṃ tātparyanirṇaye' is cited by Vedānta authors (e.g. Madhva at BSBh 1.1.4, who ascribes it to a 'Bṛhatsaṃhitā'); I did not find it as a list in the Mīmāṃsā texts consulted.

name: The six means of determining subsidiarity

definitions.definition: Direct statement, indicative power, syntactic connection, context, position and name — each later one weaker when they conflict, being more remote from the meaning (MS 3.3.14).

name: The six means of distinguishing rites

definitions.definition: A different word, repetition, number, quality, context and name (Śabara's list at MS 2.1.1; treated in adhyāya 2).

name: The six means of fixing sequence

definitions.definition: Direct statement, purpose, textual order, position, the order of principals, and the order once begun.

A subsidiary exists for another's sake (MS 3.1.2); Bādari limits subsidiaries to substances, qualities and purificatory acts, Jaimini includes acts (MS 3.1.3–4); subsidiaries help either by acting on a material or remotely toward the final apūrva.

name: For the rite or for the person

definitions.definition: An element is either for the sake of the rite or for the sake of the person; what is for the person is what gives him delight (MS 4.1.1–2). Self-knowledge is argued by Bhāṭṭas to be both (Śāstradīpikā).
Rites that lack their own procedure take it from an archetype (MS 7.4.1); transferred details are modified (ūha) or cancelled (bādha) where they serve no purpose (MS 10.1.1–2).

name: The twelve topics (lakṣaṇas) of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra

definitions.definition: Means of knowledge, distinction, subsidiarity, prompting, sequence, eligibility, general and specific transfer, modification, cancellation, single performance and incidental benefit — the subjects of the twelve adhyāyas.

A group of words is one sentence when it serves one purpose and its parts need each other if separated; otherwise the sentence splits (MS 2.1.46–47); arthavādas are one sentence with injunctions (MS 1.2.7).

Six: perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, postulation and non-apprehension; a means of knowledge apprehends the previously unapprehended and is free from causal defect and from any sublating cognition.
Five: perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison and postulation; every experience other than memory is a means of knowledge.

relations.note: dharma is known only by verbal testimony (the Veda)

definitions.definition: Supposing an unseen fact without which a seen or heard fact would be impossible — a separate means of knowledge for both Mīmāṃsā schools.

name: Non-apprehension as a means of knowledge

definitions.definition: Where no positive means of knowledge arises, non-apprehension makes known absence; absence is real and fourfold.
Not a separate means; the five suffice.
Knowledge produced by similarity: seeing the gavaya, one knows the remembered cow as similar to it.
Prior absence, absence by destruction, mutual absence and absolute absence; if absence were not real, curd would be in milk and consciousness in earth.
Validity is intrinsic (svataḥ) both in arising and in being known; invalidity is extrinsic, due to a defect in the cause or a sublating cognition.
Every experience is valid; error is a pair of cognitions not distinguished, not a false cognition.

All cognitions are valid of themselves; a capacity not present in a thing cannot be given by another; validity is set aside only by a cognition of the object's being otherwise or knowledge of a defect in the cause — neither of which can arise for the authorless Veda.
Validity is known by inferring the cognition from the knownness it produces.
Validity is known with the self-luminous cognition itself.
Validity is known by the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) of the cognition (as reported by Gaṅgeśa).

relations.note: intrinsic validity plus the absence of an author makes the Veda unassailable

definitions.definition: The Veda has no author: names of recensions come from expounders; apparent persons mentioned are sound-similarities; the unbroken chain of study has no beginning; creator-authorship is unprovable.

relations.note: a creator-author of the Veda is rejected

definitions.definition: Words, i.e. the letters, are eternal and manifested by utterance: utterance is for conveying to another; the same word is recognized everywhere; utterances are counted as repetitions; there is no cause of destruction (MS 1.1.18–23, against the view of 1.1.6–11).

relations.note: the eternal word is the letters, not a sphoṭa

name: The original relation of word and meaning

definitions.definition: The relation of word and meaning is not established by any person; it is known from the beginningless usage of elders (MS 1.1.5; Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 7).

A word means the universal (ākṛti), since action concerns it (MS 1.3.33); meanings follow the śāstra where usages differ (MS 1.3.9) and accept current usage of non-Āryas where uncontradicted (MS 1.3.10); the Buddhist 'exclusion' (apoha) is rejected.

name: How a sentence conveys its meaning

definitions.definition: Abhihitānvaya: words convey their own meanings, which then connect into the sentence meaning.
Anvitābhidhāna: words convey their meanings as already connected with one another and with what is to be done.
Letters/words convey word-meanings as an intermediate step, like the flame in cooking; the word-meanings then convey the sentence meaning.
Words are learned from elders' usage in which they occur in action-guiding sentences; hence they express meanings already connected, principally with the 'to-be-done'.
Rejected: the letters themselves (through their impressions) convey the meaning; a separate sphoṭa is unperceived and superfluous (Upavarṣa in Śabara; ŚV sphoṭavāda).
Viparītakhyāti: only the relation appearing in error is unreal; the related items are real.
Akhyāti: error is non-apprehension of the difference between a perception and a memory.
'This is silver' is two cognitions, a perception and a memory lacking its 'that', whose difference is not grasped; no cognition as such is false.
Error apprehends something as other than it is; the relation alone is unreal (Śāstradīpikā, following Kumārila; also Maṇḍana's Vibhramaviveka).

name: Knownness (jñātatā) and the inference of cognition

definitions.definition: Cognition is not perceived; it produces a property of manifestness in the object, from which it is inferred.
Every cognition is self-luminous and manifests the knower, the known and itself; the self appears only as subject.
Perception begins as a bare, non-conceptual awareness like an infant's, followed by determinate cognition of the thing with its universal etc.; both are perception.
No perception, however heightened, can know dharma: perception grasps only what is present, and any excellence of a sense stays within its own domain (seeing far or subtle, not hearing colours).

An omniscient knower of dharma is not seen now, cannot be proved to have existed, cannot be established by his own scripture without circularity, and could not be recognized by the non-omniscient; an omniscience by all six means of knowledge would not be denied, but not a perception of dharma.
A self distinct from body and cognition exists: shown by desire, memory and recognition; known to itself; taught by 'not this, not this' (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
The eternal agent and enjoyer whose existence Śabara proved against unbelief; knowing it enables rites whose fruit lies in another world, and the Upaniṣads make that knowledge firm.
Distinct from cognition, senses and body; all-pervading, permanent, many; not self-luminous, it appears as subject in each cognition and does not appear in dreamless sleep.

relations.note: in release the self remains without body, senses and objects

definitions.definition: The inner sense by which the self grasps its relation to objects and by which the self is known in saṃsāra; some Bhāṭṭas held it persists in release as the organ of the self's bliss.
The conjunction of self and mind, located in the body, is the non-inherent cause of the self's qualities; hence the self's qualities appear only where the body is.

name: Waking, dream and dreamless sleep (Mīmāṃsā view)

definitions.definition: Dreams present real objects of other times and places, remembered through impressions awakened by the unseen and taken as present by a sleep-affected mind; release resembles dreamless sleep in having no cognition, but without return.
In dreamless sleep the self is not manifest, since there is no cognition.
The world binds a person as body (seat of experience), senses (instruments) and objects (what is experienced); release is its absolute dissolution.

name: Categories (padārtha) in Mīmāṃsā

definitions.definition: Substance, quality, action, universal and absence (the later Bhāṭṭa manuals), with darkness and sound among substances.
Eight: substance, quality, action, universal, dependence (paratantratā), power (śakti), similarity (sādṛśya) and number (saṅkhyā).

notes: From memory (Mānameyodaya; Prakaraṇapañcikā's Tattvāloka); not checked here.

definitions.definition: Karma is primarily the enjoined act; its fruit comes through the apūrva; dharma and adharma produce bodies and experiences until exhausted.
Bodies arise for the experience of the fruits of karma; while dharma and adharma remain, a new body arises; when they are exhausted it does not.

Release comes by the exhaustion of karma: avoiding desire-prompted and prohibited acts, performing obligatory and occasional ones, knowing the self, and exhausting past karma by experience, so that no new body arises; release is an absence, hence permanent, not an enjoyment of pleasure (Kumārila); the absolute dissolution of the threefold bond, without bliss (Pārthasārathi); some Bhāṭṭas held that innate bliss manifests.
The absolute end of embodiment through complete exhaustion of dharma and adharma, reached by abstention, experience and self-knowledge with calm and restraint; the self remains in mere being.
The sūtra and Śabara speak of heaven as the fruit of rites; release as a goal is added by the later teachers; later Bhāṭṭas teach dharma offered to Īśvara as the cause of the highest good.

relations.note: release, being an absence, is permanent; heaven, being produced, perishes

definitions.definition: The fruit of rites for 'one desiring heaven', understood wherever no fruit is stated; the word denotes happiness (prīti) itself (Śabara); later described as happiness unmixed with sorrow, not followed by loss.

Kumārila rejects a creator Prajāpati: no means of knowledge reaches him, a bodiless being cannot will creation, compassion would create only happiness, and purposeless action is unintelligible; later Bhāṭṭas dedicate dharma to Īśvara/Govinda.
No Īśvara directs dharma and adharma or moves atoms; fruits arise from dharma and adharma with their circumstances.
The Brahma Sūtra reports Jaimini's view that dharma itself gives the fruit.

name: Creation and dissolution of the world

definitions.definition: There is no proof of a first creation or of a dissolution destroying everything; beings arise and perish continually, 'as today' (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 66–68, 113).
Things arise and perish gradually; people were always born of parents (Prakaraṇapañcikā ch. 7).

notes: Kumārila's Tantravārttika (on MS 1.3.6) nevertheless speaks of fourteen Manus in every kalpa; how this sits with ŚV 113 is not discussed in the passages checked.

definitions.definition: The deity is that to which the offering is directed, as named in injunction or mantra; the sacrificial act, not the deity, is principal and produces the fruit; the deity's embodiment and eating are not established — mantra and arthavāda statements implying them are not meant that way (MS 9.1.6–9, Śabara).
The Brahma Sūtra reports Jaimini as denying gods eligibility for certain meditations.

name: The authority of smṛti, custom and other scriptures

definitions.definition: Smṛti is authoritative as implying a Vedic source, but is set aside when it conflicts with the Veda or shows a worldly motive; customs of the good done without visible motive are authoritative (MS 1.3.1–7).
Texts of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata and the Buddhists have no authority for dharma, even where they agree with the Veda, because the sources of dharma are fixed in number (Tantravārttika).

name: Non-injury and ritual action (Mīmāṃsā view)

definitions.definition: Violence is prohibited; a rite stated as a means for one who wishes to harm (the Śyena) is harmful, and the Veda does not enjoin the harming itself.

notes: The Bhāṭṭa position that killing enjoined as part of a rite (e.g. the Agnīṣomīya animal) is not sin is general knowledge, not checked here; see dsp:sacrificial-killing.

name: The injunction of Vedic study and the transmission of the Veda

definitions.definition: The Veda is learned from a teacher by the injunction 'one's own Veda is to be studied'; after study one stays at the teacher's house to inquire into its sentences; every study presupposes an earlier teacher's study, without beginning.

name: The relation of Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā

definitions.definition: The two inquiries (into dharma and into Brahman) are distinguished; Śabara drew his proof of the self from the Śārīraka and Upavarṣa deferred it there (as reported by Śaṅkara); Kumārila says the Upaniṣads make the knowledge of the self firm; later Bhāṭṭas read Upaniṣads on the agent-self as serving rites and those on the non-transmigrating self as serving meditations.

At death the body burns with the sacrificial implements, but the self, its owner, goes to the heavenly world; the fruits of rites are enjoyed in another world, which is why knowing the self as distinct from the body matters for ritual.
